claims.text: The initial MgAlCuZnGd alloy is rapidly solidified and non-equilibrium.
The initial MgAlCuZnGd alloy contains a supersaturated solid solution.
Mg is initially distributed uniformly in the MgAlCuZnGd matrix.
The selected MgAlCuZnGd alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
Samples will be annealed at 350–400 °C for 1–10 hours in argon and compared with an as-solidified control.
Isothermal annealing causes Mg segregation and precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
The Mg-rich precipitates nucleate and grow both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Annealing transforms the metastable supersaturated solid solution into a dual-phase structure.
Mg-rich intermetallic phases provide preferential nucleation sites for MgO during high-temperature oxidation.
The precipitate-assisted MgO scale is coherent, continuous, adherent, and protective.
Formation of the proposed MgO scale enhances oxidation resistance relative to the as-solidified state.
Changes in intermetallic-phase distribution alter local electrochemical potentials and thereby influence corrosion behavior.
Intermetallic phases can act as barriers that slow corrosion-front propagation.
Electrochemical potential differences between intermetallics and an Mg matrix can also cause micro-galvanic localized corrosion.
Annealed MgAlCuZnGd samples will have a lower and more uniform saline-corrosion rate than as-solidified samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit improved high-temperature oxidation behavior at 600–700 °C relative to as-solidified controls.
The relevant corrosion behavior can be evaluated in a standardized saline solution using electrochemical measurements such as potentiodynamic polarization.
Absence of increased Mg-rich intermetallic formation, protective MgO formation, or improved oxidation and corrosion performance would falsify the proposed mechanism.
